channel.title: Junjie Chen — writing
channel.description: Notes on genomics, machine learning, and systems built on evenings.

item.title: Notes from sixty Streamlit pages
item.description: Five dashboards, sixty-odd pages, and a collection of failures that each took longer to find than they should have. A page that returns HTTP 200 while displaying a traceback, a sort order that puts 9.9% above 12.0%, and a single cached lookup that made every keystroke take ten seconds.

item.title: Choosing ten stocks out of thirty with a QUBO
item.description: Portfolio selection is a combinatorial problem hiding inside a linear-algebra costume. Posing it as a QUBO and solving it by simulated annealing takes about 200 lines of numpy — and one scaling decision that quietly decides whether any of it works.

item.title: Every backtest number I had was wrong
item.description: I went looking for one suspicious result in a strategy tournament and found that the whole leaderboard was invalid — warm-up eaten out of the window, a helper quietly re-levering every portfolio, metrics that ranked a strategy which never lost money as the worst in the field, and three days of trading that happened at the weekend.

item.title: Multi-currency is a data-modelling problem, not a formatting problem
item.description: Showing a number in a different currency looks like a display concern. It is not. Get it wrong and your history grows a step change through its middle, an FX move vanishes from a chart, and a function you wrote six months ago is still quietly answering in last year's currency.

item.title: A privacy scanner for my own repositories
item.description: I audited the repositories on my own machine and did not like what I found. The result is a stdlib-only scanner wired into every commit — and a set of design constraints that turn out to be more interesting than the regexes, starting with the fact that a scanner must not contain the things it looks for.

item.title: Bridging the bench and the model: why I'm moving toward AI for Life Science
item.description: A decade in the lab taught me how messy real biological data is. Here's why that makes me optimistic — and cautious — about machine learning in genomics, and what I want to build next.
